claim: Vibrio cholerae is a human pathogen that causes the disease cholera.
source: Vibrio cholerae, a human pathogen that causes the debilitating disease cholera, is a natural inhabitant of aquatic ecosystems (Almagro-Moreno et al., 2015; Kaper et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Almagro-Moreno et al., 2015 and Kaper et al., 1995

claim: Vibrio cholerae is a natural inhabitant of aquatic ecosystems.
source: Vibrio cholerae, a human pathogen that causes the debilitating disease cholera, is a natural inhabitant of aquatic ecosystems (Almagro-Moreno et al., 2015; Kaper et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Almagro-Moreno et al., 2015 and Kaper et al., 1995

claim: Vibrio cholerae can form biofilms on both biotic and abiotic surfaces.
source: They can form biofilms on both biotic and abiotic surfaces, which increase their infectivity and environmental survival (Donlan and Costerton, 2002; Silva and Benitez, 2016; Teschler et al., 2015; Yildiz and Visick, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Donlan and Costerton, 2002; Silva and Benitez, 2016; Teschler et al., 2015; Yildiz and Visick, 2009

claim: Biofilm formation increases Vibrio cholerae infectivity and environmental survival.
source: They can form biofilms on both biotic and abiotic surfaces, which increase their infectivity and environmental survival (Donlan and Costerton, 2002; Silva and Benitez, 2016; Teschler et al., 2015; Yildiz and Visick, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Donlan and Costerton, 2002; Silva and Benitez, 2016; Teschler et al., 2015; Yildiz and Visick, 2009

claim: The flagellum is required for biofilm formation in Escherichia coli.
source: The flagellum is required for biofilm formation in a variety of bacteria species, such as Escherichia coli (Pratt and Kolter, 1998), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (O'Toole and Kolter, 1998), and V. cholerae (Guttenplan and Kearns, 2013; Watnick and Kolter, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pratt and Kolter, 1998

claim: The flagellum is required for biofilm formation in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
source: The flagellum is required for biofilm formation in a variety of bacteria species, such as Escherichia coli (Pratt and Kolter, 1998), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (O'Toole and Kolter, 1998), and V. cholerae (Guttenplan and Kearns, 2013; Watnick and Kolter, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to O'Toole and Kolter, 1998

claim: The flagellum is required for biofilm formation in Vibrio cholerae.
source: The flagellum is required for biofilm formation in a variety of bacteria species, such as Escherichia coli (Pratt and Kolter, 1998), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (O'Toole and Kolter, 1998), and V. cholerae (Guttenplan and Kearns, 2013; Watnick and Kolter, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guttenplan and Kearns, 2013; Watnick and Kolter, 1999

claim: Mutants lacking flagella in Escherichia coli are defective for attachment.
source: Mutants lacking flagella in both E. coli and Vibrio vulnificus have been observed to be defective for attachment (Friedlander et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Friedlander et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2004

claim: Mutants lacking flagella in Vibrio vulnificus are defective for attachment.
source: Mutants lacking flagella in both E. coli and Vibrio vulnificus have been observed to be defective for attachment (Friedlander et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Friedlander et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2004

claim: Type IV pili have diverse functions including cellular twitching motility, biofilm formation, horizontal gene transfer, and host colonization.
source: Type IV pili (TFP) are another type of filamentous appendages commonly found on many bacteria and archaea, which have diverse functions such as cellular twitching motility, biofilm formation, horizontal gene transfer, and host colonization (Piepenbrink and Sundberg, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Piepenbrink and Sundberg, 2016

claim: Pseudomonas aeruginosa displays two types of TFP-driven twitching motility.
source: P. aeruginosa displays two types of TFP-driven twitching motility (Gibiansky et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gibiansky et al., 2010

claim: Neisseria gonorrhoeae shows TFP-dependent attachment leading to microcolony formation on host cell surfaces.
source: Neisseria gonorrhoeae has shown a TFP-dependent attachment, leading to the formation of microcolonies on host cell surfaces (Higashi et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Higashi et al., 2007

claim: Vibrio cholerae biosynthesizes three types of TFP that are expressed under different scenarios.
source: In contrast, although V. cholerae biosynthesizes three types of TFP that are expressed under different scenarios, they have not been observed to twitch on surfaces.
evidence: Statement made in the manuscript text

claim: Vibrio cholerae has not been observed to twitch on surfaces.
source: In contrast, although V. cholerae biosynthesizes three types of TFP that are expressed under different scenarios, they have not been observed to twitch on surfaces.
evidence: Statement made in the manuscript text

claim: The three types of pili in Vibrio cholerae are chitin-regulated competence pili (ChiRP), toxin co-regulated pili (TCP), and mannose-sensitive hemagglutinin (MSHA) TFP.
source: These three pili are chitin-regulated competence pili (ChiRP; formerly termed PilA), toxin co-regulated pili (TCP), and mannose-sensitive hemagglutinin (MSHA) TFP (Meibom et al., 2004; Reguera and Kolter, 2005; Yildiz and Visick, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Meibom et al., 2004; Reguera and Kolter, 2005; Yildiz and Visick, 2009

claim: ChiRP can grasp extracellular DNA and transport it back to the cell surface via pili retraction.
source: ChiRP were observed to be able to grasp extracellular DNA and transport it back to the cell surface via pili retraction (Ellison et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ellison et al., 2018

claim: TCP are important for host colonization and pathogenesis.
source: TCP are important for host colonization and pathogenesis (Kirn et al., 2000; Thelin and Taylor, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kirn et al., 2000; Thelin and Taylor, 1996

claim: MSHA pili are important for surface attachment of Vibrio cholerae.
source: In contrast to these two types, MSHA pili are known to be important for surface attachment of V. cholerae (Utada et al., 2014; Watnick and Kolter, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Utada et al., 2014; Watnick and Kolter, 1999

claim: Motility is a crucial element for Vibrio cholerae colonization of the epithelium leading to successful infection.
source: Motility has been shown to be a crucial element for V. cholerae colonization of the epithelium, leading to successful infection of the human host (Krukonis and DiRita, 2003; Tsou et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krukonis and DiRita, 2003; Tsou et al., 2008

claim: Two types of near-surface motility, roaming and orbiting, were observed in Vibrio cholerae.
source: Two types of near-surface motility, roaming and orbiting, were observed in V. cholera and were further suggested that V. cholerae synergistically employs the use of their flagella and MSHA pili to enable a hybrid surface motility that facilitates surface selection and attachment in aqueous environments (Utada et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Utada et al., 2014

claim: Vibrio cholerae synergistically employs flagella and MSHA pili to enable hybrid surface motility that facilitates surface selection and attachment in aqueous environments.
source: Two types of near-surface motility, roaming and orbiting, were observed in V. cholera and were further suggested that V. cholerae synergistically employs the use of their flagella and MSHA pili to enable a hybrid surface motility that facilitates surface selection and attachment in aqueous environments (Utada et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Utada et al., 2014

claim: The mucus layer of animal intestines has a wide range of viscosities, varying from the viscosity of water (~1 cP) to 1000-fold higher (1000 cP).
source: The mucus layer of animal intestines is estimated to have a wide range of viscosities, varying anywhere from the viscosity of water (~1 cP) to 1000-fold higher (1000 cP) (Lai et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lai et al., 2009

claim: MSHA pili are evenly distributed along the cell length of Vibrio cholerae.
source: The results show evenly distributed MSHA pili along the cell length, indicating the absence of preferred pili localization on the cell body.
evidence: Based on direct observation and 3D reconstruction from videos as described in the manuscript

claim: The majority of Vibrio cholerae cells have approximately 3-7 MSHA pili.
source: Quantitatively, we find that the majority of cells have approximately 3–7 MSHA pili, with 4 MSHA pili per cell being observed most frequently, as shown in Figure 1b.
evidence: Quantitative data from 110 cells shown in Figure 1b

claim: Four MSHA pili per cell is the most frequently observed number.
source: Quantitatively, we find that the majority of cells have approximately 3–7 MSHA pili, with 4 MSHA pili per cell being observed most frequently, as shown in Figure 1b.
evidence: Quantitative data from 110 cells shown in Figure 1b

claim: The number of MSHA pili per cell is positively correlated with cell length.
source: The number of MSHA pili appears to be positively correlated with cell length since it increases as the cell grows (Figure 1—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: Observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3c

claim: The number of MSHA pili shows a linear relationship with cell length.
source: Statistically, the number of MSHA pili shows a linear relationship with cell length (Figure 1c), indicating that the length density of MSHA pili is roughly constant for V. cholerae.
evidence: Statistical analysis of 368 cells shown in Figure 1c

claim: The length density of MSHA pili is roughly constant for Vibrio cholerae.
source: Statistically, the number of MSHA pili shows a linear relationship with cell length (Figure 1c), indicating that the length density of MSHA pili is roughly constant for V. cholerae.
evidence: Inferred from the linear relationship between pili number and cell length shown in Figure 1c

claim: MSHA pili growth was observed but no retraction under the experimental conditions.
source: Under our conditions, we observed MSHA pili growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 3a and b) but no retraction.
evidence: Direct observation from double-color labeling experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Wild-type Vibrio cholerae in LB+MC exhibits orbiting behavior characterized by multi-pass circular trajectories.
source: Consistent with previous reports in normal aqueous solutions (Utada et al., 2014), the WT strain in LB+MC also exhibits orbiting behavior, characterized by multi-pass circular trajectories, and roaming behavior, characterized by highly exploratory, diffusive, trajectories.
evidence: Observed behavior in experiments with LB+MC, consistent with previous reports

claim: Wild-type Vibrio cholerae in LB+MC exhibits roaming behavior characterized by highly exploratory, diffusive trajectories.
source: Consistent with previous reports in normal aqueous solutions (Utada et al., 2014), the WT strain in LB+MC also exhibits orbiting behavior, characterized by multi-pass circular trajectories, and roaming behavior, characterized by highly exploratory, diffusive, trajectories.
evidence: Observed behavior in experiments with LB+MC, consistent with previous reports

claim: Roaming cells have a radius of gyration of 19.5 μm and an average speed of 1.7 μm/s in LB+MC.
source: The roaming cell traces out a path that is linear over short distances, with a radius of gyration Rg=19.5 μm, and an average speed of 1.7 μm/s (see Figure 2a,b, Video 1).
evidence: Quantitative measurements from tracked cells shown in Figure 2a,b and Video 1

claim: Orbiting cells have a radius of gyration of 1.6 μm and an average speed of 1.1 μm/s in LB+MC.
source: In contrast, the orbiting cell trajectory is much more circular with an average Rg=1.6 μm and an average speed of 1.1 μm/s (see Figure 2c,d, Video 2).
evidence: Quantitative measurements from tracked cells shown in Figure 2c,d and Video 2

claim: Both roaming and orbiting cells make momentary pauses where their speed slows down.
source: A 3D plot of speed plotted along the trajectory in both examples show that both phenotypes make momentary pauses, where their speed slows down; this can be seen clearly in Figure 2b, where the cell motion near a surface displays a characteristic alternation between moving and stopping (Figure 2b and d).
evidence: Observed from 3D speed plots shown in Figure 2b and 2d

claim: Momentary pauses are caused by transient contact between MSHA pili and the surface.
source: However, by recording fluorescence video sequences, we directly visualized the process, thereby providing direct evidence that the pauses are due to transient contact between MSHA pili and the surface.
evidence: Direct visualization from fluorescence video sequences showing pili-surface contact

claim: MSHA pili can stretch during transient attachment to the surface.
source: In a time-lapse sequence, we show the stretching of a transiently attached pilus due to cell moving away from the point of attachment. Subsequently, this pilus detaches from the surface as the cell continues to move, as indicated with the white arrowheads in Figure 2e (for more details, see Video 2).
evidence: Direct observation from time-lapse imaging shown in Figure 2e and Video 2

claim: MSHA pili can work as a brake to abruptly slow cell motion by transiently attaching to the surface.
source: These results indicate that the MSHA pili can work as a brake to abruptly slow cell motion by transiently attaching to the surface.
evidence: Inferred from observations of pili-surface interactions and cell speed changes

claim: Different MSHA pili attach and detach dynamically, switching as the cell uses these as transient attachment points.
source: This is further confirmed by the observation that during the course of surface motion, different MSHA pili attach and detach, switching dynamically as the cell uses these as transient attachment points (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Video 3).
evidence: Direct observation from fluorescence videos shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Video 3

claim: Cell body rotation is required to balance the torque for flagellar rotation when cells swim.
source: Such a switching of the specific MSHA pili that are engaging the surface is caused by the rotation of the cell body, which is required to balance the torque for flagellar rotation when cells swim.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of bacterial swimming mechanics

claim: As the cell body rotates, different MSHA pili distributed on the cell body take turns approaching and receding from the surface.
source: Thus, as the cell body rotates due to the rotation of the flagellar motor, different MSHA pili distributed on the cell body take turns approaching and receding from the surface.
evidence: Logical inference from cell body rotation and pili distribution

claim: The switching of attached MSHA pili continues to slow down cell motion and changes the direction of motion.
source: The switching of attached MSHA pili not only continues to slow down cell motion but also changes the direction of motion.
evidence: Observed from tracking cell trajectories and pili switching events

claim: When adhesion between MSHA pili and the surface is sufficiently strong, the attachment point can act as an anchor point.
source: When the adhesion between MSHA pili and the surface is sufficiently strong, the attachment point can act as an anchor point.
evidence: Observed from cell behavior showing anchored circular motion

claim: A single anchoring MSHA pilus can deflect the trajectory of a swimming cell, bending linear motion into circular motion centered around the attachment point.
source: We demonstrate this by showing the deflection of the trajectory of a swimming cell by the attachment of a single anchoring MSHA pilus; here, linear motion is bent into a circular motion that is centered around the attachment point (see Video 4).
evidence: Direct observation from Video 4 showing trajectory deflection

claim: The upper bound for the force exerted on the pilus during anchored circular motion is estimated to be ~50 pN in LB+MC.
source: The force on the pilus will be less than this upper bound, partly due to the difference in direction between the pilus force and the propulsion force, which helps the cell rotate around the anchor point. Cell body rotations are an order of magnitude slower in the LB+MC solution used here than in water, so we estimate the flagellar rotation rate to be in the range of 10–100 rad/s. The viscosity of LB+MC is ~0.2 Pa⋅s and this gives us an upper bound for the force on the pilus of ~50 pN.
evidence: Calculated using resistive force theory model from Lauga et al., 2006

claim: The upper bound for the force exerted on the pilus during anchored circular motion is estimated to be ~3 pN in water.
source: In water, we estimate an upper bound of ~3 pN.
evidence: Calculated using resistive force theory model

claim: The estimated forces on pili are smaller than the 100 pN forces that pili can sustain.
source: These estimates are smaller than the 100 pN forces that pili can sustain (Maier et al., 2002).
evidence: Comparison with known pili force tolerance from Maier et al., 2002

claim: The anchoring of MSHA pilus eventually leads to the irreversible attachment of the cell.
source: The anchoring of MSHA pilus eventually leads to the irreversible attachment of the cell.
evidence: Observed from tracking cells through complete landing sequence

claim: The landing process of Vibrio cholerae includes three phases: running, lingering, and attaching.
source: Based on the pattern of motion displayed by the cell (Figure 3a and Video 5), we divide the landing process into three phases: running, lingering, and attaching.
evidence: Classification based on observed cell behavior patterns shown in Figure 3a and Video 5

claim: In the running phase, cells swim and can perform roaming or orbiting.
source: In the running phase (0–3.77 s), cells will swim and can perform roaming or orbiting.
evidence: Observed behavior during the running phase

claim: Misalignments between the flagellum and cell body axis tend to change the motion direction of the cell.
source: We note that misalignments between the flagellum and cell body axis tend to change the motion direction of the cell (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: Observed from simultaneous imaging of flagellum and cell body shown in Figure 3a,b

claim: In the lingering phase, cells demonstrate either a paused state or a tethered state.
source: In the lingering phase (3.77–4.68 s), the cells demonstrate one of two states: a paused state or a tethered state, where the cell can move under the constraint of tethering pilus (see Figure 3a for the tethered state).
evidence: Observed behavior during the lingering phase shown in Figure 3a

claim: In the attaching phase, cells remain on the surface motionless during the observation period.
source: Finally, in the attaching phase (≥ 4.68 s), cells remain on the surface motionless during the observation period most likely since they have effected irreversible attachment.
evidence: Observed behavior during the attaching phase

claim: Upon irreversible cell attachment, some free MSHA pili become attached to the surface firmly while others demonstrate fluctuations punctuated with intermittent attachment.
source: Upon irreversible cell attachment, some of the free MSHA pili become attached to the surface firmly while others demonstrate fluctuations punctuated with intermittent attachment to the surface (Video 6).
evidence: Direct observation from Video 6

claim: Transitions between the running and lingering phases are observed during cell landing.
source: During cell landing, transitions between the running and lingering phases, as well as between the two states of the lingering phase are observed, respectively.
evidence: Observed from tracking cells through landing sequence

claim: The running phase has a relatively lower transition probability to the tethered state (~22%) but a higher probability to the paused state (~78%).
source: The measured conditional probabilities qij that cell transitions from state i to j show that the running phase has a relatively lower qrt to the tethered state (~22%) but a higher qrp to the paused state (~78%).
evidence: Calculated from 666 transition events

claim: The paused state has a higher transition probability back to running than to tethering.
source: Similarly, the paused state has a higher qpr than qpt.
evidence: Calculated from transition event data

claim: The tethered state shows similar transition probabilities to running and paused states, which are 45% and 55%, respectively.
source: In contrast, the tethered state shows similar qtr and qtp, which are 45% and 55%, respectively (Figure 3c).
evidence: Calculated from transition event data shown in Figure 3c

claim: The period for body rotation in the running phase is generally distributed between 0.25 and 2 s and is centered at ~0.7 s in LB+MC.
source: In the running phase of V. cholerae, we found that the period for body rotation is generally distributed between 0.25 and 2 s and is centered at ~0.7 s (the rotation rate was ~1.5 Hz) in LB+MC (Figure 4a).
evidence: Statistical analysis of 416 rotation events from 54 cells shown in Figure 4a

claim: The rotation rate of the cell body in the running phase is ~1.5 Hz in LB+MC.
source: In the running phase of V. cholerae, we found that the period for body rotation is generally distributed between 0.25 and 2 s and is centered at ~0.7 s (the rotation rate was ~1.5 Hz) in LB+MC (Figure 4a).
evidence: Calculated from rotation period data shown in Figure 4a

claim: Swimming speed linearly increases with cell body rotation rate with a slope of |v/ωc|=2.48±0.04 μm/radian.
source: By fitting the data, we found that v linearly increases with ωc with a slope of |v/ωc|=2.48±0.04 μm/radian.
evidence: Linear fit of measured data from 47 cells shown in Figure 4b

claim: A cell in the tethered state typically performs a circular motion around the attachment point.
source: By contrast, a cell in the tethered state typically performs a circular motion around the attachment point (red dots in Figure 4c).
evidence: Direct observation from tracking tethered cells shown in Figure 4c

claim: The direction of circular motion in the tethered state can switch from counterclockwise to clockwise.
source: The direction of the circular motion is also dynamic and can switch from counterclockwise (CCW) to clockwise (CW) presumably due to a switch in the rotation direction of the flagellar motor (see 2.6 s, Figure 4c).
evidence: Direct observation from tracking tethered cells shown in Figure 4c and Video 7

claim: Angular velocity is roughly constant during each circular-motion interval in the tethered state.
source: Angular velocity is roughly constant during each circular-motion interval (i.e., in each CCW or CW period) and quickly changes sign after CCW-CW switching (Figure 4d and Video 7).
evidence: Measured from tracking tethered cell motion shown in Figure 4d and Video 7

claim: Tethering can occur at a pole or under the body, leading to cells standing vertically or lying down horizontally to the surface.
source: Due to the distribution of pili across the cell body, tethering can occur at a pole or under the body, which leads to cells standing vertically or lying down horizontally to the surface, respectively.
evidence: Observed from different tethering configurations

claim: Standing tethered cells perform faster circular motion (mean angular speed=8.5±1.9 rad/s) than lying ones (mean angular speed=3.0±2.1 rad/s).
source: We find that standing tethered cells perform a faster circular motion (mean angular speed=8.5±1.9 rad/s) than lying ones (mean angular speed=3.0±2.1 rad/s) (Figure 4e).
evidence: Statistical analysis of 38 vertical tethering intervals from 5 cells and 241 horizontal tethering intervals from 25 cells shown in Figure 4e

claim: MSHA pili appear to be able to attach to the surface along their entire length, not just the tip.
source: In addition to the fact that unattached pili may increase the likelihood that the cell will make the irreversible attachment, we observe that MSHA pili appear to be able to attach to the surface along their entire length, and not just the tip (Video 8).
evidence: Direct observation from Video 8 showing pilus attachment along its length

claim: The flagellum of attached cells frequently continues to rotate after cell attachment.
source: Interestingly, we find that the flagellum of attached cells frequently continues to rotate (Video 5, after 4.68 s), indicating that even after cell attachment, the flagellar motor is still active for some period.
evidence: Direct observation from Video 5

claim: The flagellum will eventually stop rotating after a cell stays long enough on the surface.
source: The flagellum will eventually stop rotating after a cell stays long enough on the surface (Video 9).
evidence: Direct observation from Video 9

claim: LB+MC is a non-Newtonian fluid with shear-dependent viscosity.
source: Rheological measurements show that its viscosity is shear dependent and has a higher storage modulus than loss modulus in the tested oscillation frequency range; thus, it is a non-Newtonian fluid (Figure 6a–c).
evidence: Rheological measurements shown in Figure 6a-c

claim: An 18.7% (w/w) mucin solution in 2% LB shows similar viscoelastic behavior to LB+MC with a higher storage modulus than loss modulus.
source: On the other hand, the rheological measurements of an 18.7% (w/w) mucin solution in 2% LB, which was obtained by measuring the concentration of mixtures scraped from the fresh mouse intestine surfaces, show similar viscoelastic behavior with a higher storage modulus than loss modulus in the same tested oscillation frequency range (Figure 6d–f).
evidence: Rheological measurements shown in Figure 6d-f

claim: LB+MC better simulates the viscoelastic environment that Vibrio cholerae cells encounter in the mucus layer of animal intestines compared to Ficoll solutions.
source: Therefore, compared with Ficoll solutions, which are Newtonian fluids, LB+MC better simulates the viscoelastic environment that V. cholerae cells encounter in the mucus layer of animal intestines.
evidence: Based on comparison of rheological properties between LB+MC, Ficoll, and actual mucin solutions

claim: Wild-type cells demonstrate roaming and orbiting motilities in both 2% LB and LB+MC solutions.
source: We observed WT cells to demonstrate roaming and orbiting motilities in both solutions (Figure 5a).
evidence: Direct observation from cell tracking shown in Figure 5a

claim: The roaming and orbiting motilities of cells are robust against the tested viscoelastic environment.
source: These results indicate that the roaming and orbiting motilities of cells are robust against the tested viscoelastic environment.
evidence: Observed similar motility patterns in both 2% LB and LB+MC

claim: The average speed of WT cells for near-surface motion is reduced by ~22 times from 86.7±32.9 μm/s in 2% LB to 3.8±2.6 μm/s in LB+MC.
source: The average speed of WT cells for near-surface motion is reduced by ~22 times from 86.7±32.9 μm/s (mean ± standard deviation) in 2% LB to 3.8±2.6 μm/s in LB+MC.
evidence: Measured from cell tracking data

claim: The average speed of △mshA cells is decreased by ~12 times from 80.0±15.0 μm/s in 2% LB to 6.5±1.4 μm/s in LB+MC.
source: Similarly, the average speed of △mshA cells is also decreased by ~12 times from 80.0±15.0 μm/s in 2% LB to 6.5±1.4 μm/s in LB+MC.
evidence: Measured from cell tracking data

claim: In LB+MC, WT cells tend to land on the surface soon after approaching it and show more tethered motion.
source: In LB+MC, WT cells tend to land on the surface soon after approaching it (less than one round in orbiting motility) and more tethered motion is observed, which leads to more irregular and tortuous trajectories and smaller Rg for WT cells compared with the case of 2% LB (Figure 5c).
evidence: Observed from cell trajectories and Rg distributions shown in Figure 5c

claim: △mshA cells show very similar Rg distributions in 2% LB and LB+MC.
source: By contrast, △mshA cells show very similar Rg distributions in the two types of solutions (Figure 5c).
evidence: Statistical analysis shown in Figure 5c

claim: In LB+MC, a large proportion of △mshA cells show orbiting for a substantial number of cycles.
source: More interestingly, compared with WT, in LB+MC, a large proportion of △mshA cells show orbiting for a substantial number of cycles, as shown in Figure 5b.
evidence: Observed from cell trajectories shown in Figure 5b

claim: The loss of MSHA pili results in a significant increase in mean path length in LB+MC relative to 2% LB.
source: This shows that the loss of MSHA pili results in a significant increase in mean path length in LB+MC relative to 2% LB.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of path length ratios between LB+MC and 2% LB

claim: Prolonged orbiting motions of △mshA were not observed in a 20% Ficoll solution.
source: Moreover, such prolonged orbiting motions of △mshA were not observed in a 20% Ficoll solution (Figure 5), which has a high viscosity but still belongs to the class of Newtonian fluids (Winet, 1976).
evidence: Observed from cell trajectories in 20% Ficoll shown in Figure 5, with citation to Winet, 1976

claim: The average cell speed for near-surface motion is 9.3±4.3 μm/s for WT and 10.0±3.5 μm/s for △mshA in 20% Ficoll.
source: As shown in Figure 5, the cell motility behaviors in 20% Ficoll are similar to those in 2% LB only except that the average cell speed for near-surface motion is dramatically lower in 20% Ficoll, which is 9.3±4.3 μm/s for WT and 10.0±3.5 μm/s for △mshA.
evidence: Measured from cell tracking data

claim: The elastic properties of viscoelastic solutions can affect cell motility behavior.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the elastic properties of viscoelastic solutions can also affect cell motility behavior and the role of MSHA pili as a braking and anchoring machine in cell landing is more apparent in viscoelastic (non-Newtonian) fluids than in viscous Newtonian fluids.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of cell behavior in LB+MC, 2% LB, and 20% Ficoll

claim: The role of MSHA pili as a braking and anchoring machine in cell landing is more apparent in viscoelastic (non-Newtonian) fluids than in viscous Newtonian fluids.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the elastic properties of viscoelastic solutions can also affect cell motility behavior and the role of MSHA pili as a braking and anchoring machine in cell landing is more apparent in viscoelastic (non-Newtonian) fluids than in viscous Newtonian fluids.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of path length ratios in different fluid types

claim: The first step in Vibrio cholerae biofilm formation is the transition from planktonic swimmers to stationary surface-attached cells.
source: The first step in V. cholerae biofilm formation is the transition from planktonic swimmers to the stationary surface-attached cells; this process is mediated by the landing process (Teschler et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Teschler et al., 2015

claim: During near-surface swimming, hydrodynamic forces cause the cell bodies of swimming rod-like bacteria to take on a tilted, non-parallel orientation to the surface.
source: During near-surface swimming, it has been suggested that hydrodynamic forces cause the cell bodies of swimming rod-like bacteria to take on a tilted, non-parallel, orientation to the surface (Vigeant et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vigeant et al., 2002

claim: In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, TFP are distributed with a strong bias toward a particular pole.
source: In the case of P. aeruginosa, whose TFP are distributed with a strong bias toward a particular pole (Skerker and Berg, 2001), pili-surface contact will depend on which pole is closer to the surface.
evidence: Supported by citation to Skerker and Berg, 2001

claim: The homogeneous distribution of MSHA pili on Vibrio cholerae may be more efficient at slowing tilted cell bodies by increasing the probability that pili encounter the surface.
source: In contrast, the homogeneous distribution of MSHA pili on V. cholerae (see Figure 1c) may be more efficient at slowing such tilted cell bodies by increasing the probability that pili encounter the surface relative to bacteria with biased pili distributions.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with P. aeruginosa and consideration of pili distribution effects

claim: Cells rotating at an angle closer to the surface have a slower angular velocity.
source: Cells rotating at an angle closer to the surface have a slower angular velocity (Figure 4e), to which hydrodynamic effects presumably have an important contribution (Bennett et al., 2016).
evidence: Observed from data in Figure 4e, with citation to Bennett et al., 2016

claim: Progressive twisting of the surface-attached pilus fiber during circular motion may gradually cause the circular motion to stop by pulling the cell body closer to the surface.
source: This suggests that for cells demonstrating tethered motion, a progressive twisting of the surface-attached pilus fiber during the circular motion of cells may gradually cause the circular motion to stop by pulling the cell body ever closer to the surface.
evidence: Speculative mechanism inferred from observed tethered motion dynamics

claim: Twitching has not been observed in Vibrio cholerae under the experimental conditions.
source: Although twitching has not to be observed in V. cholerae, this is one mechanism by which retraction-like dynamics may be achieved (Charles et al., 2019), possibly in tandem with actual retraction of MSHA pili, which has been shown recently in a different strain of V. cholera (Floyd et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement of observation with citations to Charles et al., 2019 and Floyd et al., 2020

claim: MSHA pili retraction has been shown in a different strain of Vibrio cholerae.
source: Although twitching has not to be observed in V. cholerae, this is one mechanism by which retraction-like dynamics may be achieved (Charles et al., 2019), possibly in tandem with actual retraction of MSHA pili, which has been shown recently in a different strain of V. cholera (Floyd et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Floyd et al., 2020

claim: Under the experimental conditions, MSHA pili retraction events were not observed.
source: Under our conditions, we have not observed MSHA pili retraction events nor have we seen bacterial cells that gradually acquire fluorescence when only maleimide dyes were used.
evidence: Direct observation from experiments

claim: In bacteria where pilus retraction occurs, the cell body gradually becomes fluorescent due to internalization of labeled pilin by retraction.
source: These results are consistent since in bacteria where pilus retraction does occur, such as in the TAD pili of C. crescentus (Ellison et al., 2017), ChiRP of V. cholera (Ellison et al., 2018), and TFP of P. aeruginosa (Skerker and Berg, 2001), the cell body gradually becomes fluorescent due to internalization of labeled pilin by retraction.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ellison et al., 2017; Ellison et al., 2018; Skerker and Berg, 2001

claim: The ability of MSHA pili to adhere along their entire length contrasts with TFP of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which show pilus-subject interactions mainly mediated by the pilus tip.
source: The ability to adhere not only at the distal tip, contrasts with the TFP of P. aeruginosa (Skerker and Berg, 2001) and ChiRP of V. cholerae (Ellison et al., 2018), which show that the pilus-subject interactions are mainly mediated by the pilus tip.
evidence: Comparison with cited studies on P. aeruginosa and ChiRP

claim: The ability of MSHA pili to adhere along their entire length contrasts with ChiRP of Vibrio cholerae, which show pilus-subject interactions mainly mediated by the pilus tip.
source: The ability to adhere not only at the distal tip, contrasts with the TFP of P. aeruginosa (Skerker and Berg, 2001) and ChiRP of V. cholerae (Ellison et al., 2018), which show that the pilus-subject interactions are mainly mediated by the pilus tip.
evidence: Comparison with cited study on ChiRP

claim: Vibrio cholerae cells can enhance adhesion strength by increasing both the segment length and the number of MSHA pili adhered to the surface.
source: Rather, cells can enhance the adhesion strength by increasing both the segment length and the number of MSHA pili adhered to the surface.
evidence: Inferred from observation that pili can adhere along their length

claim: Increasing pilus adhesion segment length and number facilitates irreversible attachment in Vibrio cholerae.
source: These two effects will facilitate irreversible attachment in V. cholerae.
evidence: Inferred from the ability to enhance adhesion strength

claim: Similar running and lingering phases in near-surface motion have been reported in enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) cells.
source: Similar running and lingering phases in near-surface motion have also been reported in enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) cells (Perez Ipiña et al., 2019), where the results suggest that by choosing the optimal transition rates, EHEC bacterial diffusivity is maximized and surface exploration efficiency is greatly improved.
evidence: Supported by citation to Perez Ipiña et al., 2019

claim: By choosing optimal transition rates, EHEC bacterial diffusivity is maximized and surface exploration efficiency is greatly improved.
source: Similar running and lingering phases in near-surface motion have also been reported in enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) cells (Perez Ipiña et al., 2019), where the results suggest that by choosing the optimal transition rates, EHEC bacterial diffusivity is maximized and surface exploration efficiency is greatly improved.
evidence: Supported by citation to Perez Ipiña et al., 2019

claim: Vibrio cholerae motility exhibits a regiospecific influence on colonization in the small intestine.
source: In such viscoelastic environments, Millet et al., 2014 observed considerable differences of bacterial localization in different parts of the small intestine and found that V. cholerae motility exhibits a regiospecific influence on colonization, indicating that viscoelastic intestinal mucin is a key factor limiting colonization.
evidence: Supported by citation to Millet et al., 2014

claim: Viscoelastic intestinal mucin is a key factor limiting Vibrio cholerae colonization.
source: In such viscoelastic environments, Millet et al., 2014 observed considerable differences of bacterial localization in different parts of the small intestine and found that V. cholerae motility exhibits a regiospecific influence on colonization, indicating that viscoelastic intestinal mucin is a key factor limiting colonization.
evidence: Supported by citation to Millet et al., 2014

claim: MSHA pili can stick to surfaces at any point along the filament.
source: The results show that MSHA pili are evenly distributed along the cell length and can stick to surfaces at any point along the filament.
evidence: Observed from fluorescence videos showing pili-surface interactions

claim: MSHA pili act as a brake and anchor during cell landing.
source: With such properties, MSHA pili are observed to act as a brake and anchor during cell landing which includes three phases: running, lingering, and attaching.
evidence: Observed from tracking cells through landing sequence

claim: Loss of MSHA pili results in a more dramatic increase in mean path length in LB+MC than in 2% LB only or in 20% Ficoll solutions.
source: Importantly, loss of MSHA pili results in a more dramatic increase in mean path length in LB+MC than in 2% LB only or in 20% Ficoll solutions, indicating that the role of MSHA pili during cell landing is more apparent in viscoelastic non-Newtonian fluids than viscous Newtonian ones.
evidence: Calculated from comparison of path length ratios in different fluid types

claim: Typical MSHA pili are ~0.4–1.2 μm in length.
source: Typical MSHA pili are ~0.4–1.2 μm in length.
evidence: Measured from fluorescence imaging of labeled pili

claim: The cysteine substitution-based labeling method is specific and has been successfully applied to visualize TAD pili of Caulobacter crescentus and TFP of Vibrio cholerae.
source: Among them, the cysteine substitution-based labeling method is specific and has been successfully applied to visualize tight adherence (TAD) pili of Caulobacter crescentus and TFP of V. cholera (Ellison et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ellison et al., 2019

claim: MshAT70C displays similar hemagglutination behavior to wild-type, indicating that the point mutation does not affect MSHA pilus function.
source: The results of the hemagglutination assay test show that MshAT70C displays similar behavior to WT, which indicates that the point mutation in MSHA does not affect MSHA pilus function (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Hemagglutination assay results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4

claim: The viscosity of LB+MC is ~0.2 Pa⋅s.
source: The viscosity of LB+MC is ~0.2 Pa⋅s and this gives us an upper bound for the force on the pilus of ~50 pN.
evidence: Measured from rheological experiments

claim: 2% LB is a Newtonian fluid with a viscosity ~1 cP at 30℃.
source: To further investigate the dependence of MSHA pili function and hence cell landing on viscoelasticity, we compared cell motion behavior (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1) obtained in 2% LB, which is a Newtonian fluid with a viscosity ~1 cP at 30℃ (Utada et al., 2014) and in 2% LB+1% MC, which is a non-Newtonian fluid and has a shear-dependent viscosity (Figure 6), for both WT and △mshA cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Utada et al., 2014
